opening.headline: When you get an incorrect answer and don't know the cause, classifying the failed response as missing, made up, or formatting error will narrow down your suspicions.
body: We've received ten reports of assistants giving incorrect answers, some missing information, some saying things that aren't there, and some using different formats. If you look at this all at once as 'the guidelines are the problem', you miss the point of fixing it.

In this class, you will learn the criteria for dividing failures into three types: omissions, inventions, and formal errors. Practice asking discrimination questions as you go through the process of classifying ten failure responses, and organize which cause candidates come to mind for each type.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the characteristics of omissions, inventions, and formatting errors
Failure responses can be classified into types:

screens.title: The answer is wrong, but the cause cannot be classified.
screens.lead: First, read the situation of the team that has accumulated incorrect answer reports.

visual.alt: Illustration of ten incorrect answer reports stacked in a pile, waiting to be divided into three sections.

paragraphs: We received ten reports of a team receiving the wrong answer for an assistant they created. As I read, some answers were missing necessary information, some were saying things without evidence, and some answers were correct, but came out as sentences that were not in the requested table.

If we look at these ten cases all at once as 'the guidelines are the problem', we miss the point of fixing them. Problems with missing information cannot be solved by revising the instructions, and format problems cannot be solved by changing the materials.
So first, divide the wrong answers into types. Dividing the types narrows down the cause candidates and provides an order in which to start checking.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If the fact that it was wrong is the same, but the way it was done is different, can the way to fix it be the same?

screens.outro: When I see a wrong answer, I will remember where I started.

screens.title: Where do I start when I see an incorrect answer?
screens.lead: If you first think about each item in your head and then select it, the instructor will organize your thoughts. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Is the question itself your first doubt?
items.answer: If your question is ambiguous, your assistant may answer in the wrong direction. However, if the question is clear but incorrect, the next clue lies in the answer itself. The starting point for classification is to see what is missing from the answer, what has been added, and what form it takes.

items.prompt: Which do you fix first: the references or the instructions?
items.answer: Many people change the instructions first. However, if you just change the instructions without information in the reference materials, there will be no improvement. It is necessary to look at the symptoms and select the place to suspect.

items.prompt: Have you checked to see if the connected app is being imported properly?
items.answer: If an app or file isn't read properly, Assistant will only respond with the information it has. Symptoms at this time usually appear as answers with missing information.

screens.outro: Now let's look at how to distinguish between the three types of failure.

screens.title: Three types of failure
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what omissions, inventions, and formatting errors look like.

tabs.label: missing
tabs.body: Required information is missing from the response. For example, this answer only talks about the return period and omits the application method and basis provisions. What was said is correct, but the characteristic is that facts that must be included in the expected response criteria are omitted.

tabs.label: made up
tabs.body: This is a case where information that is not in the supporting materials is stated as fact, and is also called hallucination. For example, the answer refers to an extension period that is not specified in the regulations. Even if the format is correct and the sentence is natural, if there is no basis, it is made up. This is the most difficult type to recognize because it looks plausible.

tabs.label: format error
tabs.body: The content is correct, but it is different from the requested format or structure. A typical example is when you asked for a table but the answer was given in sentences. Since the facts are not wrong, it is easy to overlook it if you only read the content. However, this will be an unusable answer for users who receive the table and try to paste it right away. Also check the formal conditions in your request as part of your criteria.

tabs.label: In case of overlap
tabs.body: Two types can overlap in one response. For example, information is missing and the answer is formatted incorrectly. In this case, instead of forcing yourself to choose one, mark both types and look at each candidate cause separately.

screens.outro: Now that you know the types, let's practice classifying actual failure responses.

screens.title: Classify ten failed responses by type
screens.lead: Select the arrows to follow the sequential decision questions your instructor asks as he sorts through each failed response.

steps.title: Preparation: Set the standard aside
steps.body: Classification requires criteria. For each question, write down the expected response criteria - the facts that must be included and the required format - next to the response. Without standards, it's difficult to move beyond feeling 'weird'.

steps.title: Determination 1: Are criteria facts missing?
steps.body: If any of the facts in the expected response criteria are not included in the response, it is an omission. This is a case where the application method or basis provisions are missing.

steps.title: Determination 2: Is the response based on facts?
steps.body: If the facts in your response are not in the supporting material, you are making it up. Since you will need to cross-check against supporting evidence, it is helpful to have a prompt document guide you through this. When dealing with long documents, it is easier to determine whether the response is based on the document by having the person quote the relevant part first and then respond.

steps.title: Determination 3: Is the facts correct, but the format is different?
steps.body: If all the facts are in the base and nothing is missing, but the format is different from the requested format, it is a format error. Prompt documents specify the output format and encourage you to say what to do rather than what not to do.

steps.title: Tally: Count each cell
steps.body: After classification, count the number of items by type. By addressing the most common types first, you can reduce more failures with one fix.

screens.outro: Now let's see how type narrows down cause candidates with an example response.

screens.title: Type narrows down the cause
screens.lead: Below is the request I made and the three responses for illustrative purposes. Selecting a highlighted passage will reveal what type of response it is and possible causes for suspicion.

data.text:
Request: Please provide a table showing the return period and application method, along with the relevant clause.  
Answer A: Returns are accepted within 7 days of receipt.  
Response B: Returns are possible within 7 days after delivery, as specified in Extended to 14 days until the end of the year. Applications can be made through the app.  
Answer C: Returns must be made within 7 days of receipt, and requests can be made in the order history of the app. The basis is Article 5.

marks.span: Answer A: Returns are accepted within 7 days of receipt.
marks.note: It's missing. The application method and grounds provisions are missing. The cause of doubt is whether the information is missing from the reference material or whether the assistant is not reading the material properly. Knowledge files are reference material, not rules.

marks.span: Extended to 14 days until the end of the year
marks.note: It's made up. The extension period, which was not in the supporting materials, was stated as fact. The place to be suspicious is whether you were instructed to answer that you don't know when there is no evidence.

marks.span: Answer C: Returns must be made within 7 days of receipt, and requests can be made in the order history of the app.
marks.note: Format error. In fact, it is true and there is a supporting clause, but I answered in sentences rather than tables. Where to be suspicious is if the formal instructions are vague or illustrative.

This section shows that response C is not an omission in that it meets the requested supporting provisions. When dividing into types, check each part of the response separately to ensure it meets the criteria.

screens.outro: Now that we know the candidate causes, let's read the results of the ten response classifications.

screens.title: Commentary: Read the results of the ten responses categorized
screens.lead: The instructor explains the results of categorizing the first ten failed responses to the problem. These results are an example for illustrative purposes only. Select the arrow to move on.

steps.title: View classification results at a glance
steps.body: After classifying the ten cases, they were divided into four cases of omission, two cases of fabrication, and four cases of formatting errors. The initial assumption that ‘it was all a guidance matter’ was not correct.

steps.title: 4 missing
steps.body: All four omissions were questions about recent policies. Since the commonalities are clear, the candidate causes are also narrowed down. It is likely that the reference does not have a recent policy or the file is unreadable.

steps.title: 2 made up
steps.body: The two cases of making things up involved making up dates to answer questions that were not in the data. One candidate comes to mind: there is no instruction to answer a question you don't know.

steps.title: 4 format errors
steps.body: The four formatting errors involved answering in sentences when asked to answer in a table. This is a type that gets better if you specify the table format specifically and provide examples.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: Omissions and formatting errors are the most common, with four each. Because the places to fix are different for the two types, they are not fixed all at once, but are fixed one by one and then checked again. Even if the number of cases is small, fabrications have a large impact on trust, so separate responses are prepared.

screens.outro: Let’s pair the cause candidates by type one more time.

screens.title: Commentary: Pairing cause candidates by type
screens.lead: When you select each type, the instructor's commentary will unfold. Please note that candidate causes are hypotheses, not confirmations.

items.prompt: Omission → What cause candidates come to mind?
items.answer: The most recent policy is not in the data, or the data cannot be read by the assistant. GPT's knowledge is that it is a reference to get information from a file, so if the file is out of date or in a difficult-to-read format, it will fail to respond. Text-centered files are better used than files with complex layouts.

items.prompt: Made up → What cause candidates come to mind?
items.answer: It is possible that they were not instructed to say that they did not know when they did not know. If you are allowed to answer without evidence, you can fill in the blanks with something plausible.

items.prompt: Formal error → Which cause candidates come to mind?
items.answer: It is possible that format instructions and examples were lacking. It often gets better if you specify the format specifically and show an example or two.

items.prompt: Are these candidates a confirmed cause?
items.answer: No. Candidates are hypotheses. After you fix one, you should check again with the same question to see if it really has improved. If there is no improvement, move on to the next candidate.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Type narrows down the cause
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.

paragraphs: Incorrect answers can be divided into three types: omissions, inventions, and formatting errors. Set aside the expected response criteria and ask in turn whether there are any missing facts, unfounded facts, or whether the facts are correct but in a different format.

Once the type is determined, the areas of suspicion are narrowed down. However, this is a hypothesis, not a confirmation, so you need to correct one place and check again with the same question. Just as the presumption in the first problem that it was 'all a guideline problem' was wrong, classification changes the presumption into evidence.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Divide incorrect answers by type first. The type narrows down the cause candidates, and the candidates are checked and verified again.

checks.q: The date written in the response is not found anywhere in the supporting materials. The content also fits the tabular format request. What type of failure is this?
checks.explain: If the facts of the answer are not in the supporting data, it is a fabrication. Even if the format is correct, unfounded content is a separate problem.

wrong.0: An omission is when required information is missing from the response, but here the missing information has been added.
wrong.1: I said the format is correct, so it's not a format error.
wrong.3: Since the unfounded date was stated as fact, it cannot be considered normal.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match failure types with possible cause candidates
right: Don't tell people to say they don't know when they don't know.
The latest policy is not in the data or the file cannot be read.
Lack of format instructions and examples
checks.explain: Since the candidate cause is a hypothesis, it must be modified and then checked again with the same question.
checks.intro: Try to organize the concepts and explanations by pairing them. Results are not recorded.

glossary.def: This is a failure type where required information is missing from the response.
This is a type of failure to say something that is not in the evidence as fact.
This is a type of failure where the content is correct but the format or structure is different from the requested one.
It is a correspondence that narrows down the components to suspect based on the type of failure.

misconceptions.myth: All the wrong answers are made up.
misconceptions.fact: There are also many omissions and formatting errors. It is common to feel that something is wrong because information is missing or is not in the format requested.
Types may overlap in one response, and each type may have different causes even in one assistant.

misconceptions.myth: As long as the type is known, the cause can be determined.
misconceptions.fact: What the type tells us is the candidate cause. After making corrections, you must check again with the same question.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Failure responses are divided into three types: omissions, inventions, and formatting errors.
The type narrows down the cause candidates.
Since the candidate is a hypothesis, it is revised and checked again.
We cover the most common types first.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What types of failures does my assistant see most often?

title: Failure types: omissions, fabrications, and formatting errors
